lede: Some differences between people come in a few separate kinds; others come in every size in between. One question, counted or measured, decides the name of the variation and the graph you draw. Then there is where the differences come from: genes, the environment, or both.
can: Decide whether a characteristic shows continuous or discontinuous variation, and say why.
Choose and read the right graph, and turn a reading into a percentage of the class.
Explain the genetic and environmental causes of variation, including what a mutation is.

md: **Variation** is the differences between individuals in their **phenotype**, the characteristics each one actually has. It comes in two types.

**Discontinuous variation** falls into a few **separate groups**, with nothing in between: **tongue rolling** and **hand dominance** are the examples. **Continuous variation** can take **any value in a range**: **height** and **length** are the examples. You measure them, and every value in between is possible.

stem: A class records two things about each pupil: whether their earlobes are free or attached, and the length of their index finger. State the type of variation each shows, and give a reason for each. [4]

steps.decision: Ask one question: counted into groups, or measured on a scale? Earlobes are sorted into groups.

steps.working: Every pupil is in one of two separate groups, free or attached, with nothing in between.
steps.decision: The reason names the groups and says there is nothing between them.
A finger's length is measured with a ruler.

steps.working: It can take any value in a range: between any two lengths there is always another.
steps.decision: The reason is the phrase the scheme credits: any value in a range.

prompt: Thumb length is measured in millimetres and can be any value in a range. Which type of variation does it show?
explain: Ask the question the worked answer asked: counted into groups, or measured on a scale? Thumb length is measured, and between any two lengths there is always another, as finger length was in steps 3 and 4. So it is continuous variation.

optionNotes.why: Discontinuous is for characteristics sorted into a few separate groups, like tongue rolling; a length can be any value, so it is continuous.

twin.prompt: Eye colour is recorded as brown, blue or green. Which type of variation does it show?
twin.explain: Counted into groups, or measured? Eye colour is recorded as one of a few separate groups, with nothing in between, as the earlobes were in steps 1 and 2. So it is discontinuous variation.

md: Draw the graph the data already has in it. Blood groups are separate boxes: there is no blood group between A and B, so a **bar chart** leaves **gaps** between its bars. Height is a scale: between any two heights there is always another, so a **histogram** has its **bars touching**, each class running straight into the next.

title: Where a height on a boundary goes
md: Each class runs from its lower value up to, but not including, its upper value. A height of exactly 165 cm goes in the 165 to 170 class, so every height has exactly one place and no gap is left.

stem: The same class wants to display its earlobe results and its finger lengths. Name the type of graph for each, and give a reason. [4]

steps.working: Earlobes: a bar chart, its bars standing apart.
steps.decision: Separate groups have nothing between them, so the bars do not touch.

steps.working: Because earlobe type falls into separate groups.
steps.decision: Give the reason from the data, not from the graph.

steps.working: Finger length: a histogram, whose bars touch.
steps.decision: Measured lengths go into classes of equal width that run straight into one another.

steps.working: Because finger length is continuous: it can take any value.
steps.decision: The same reason as for the type of variation.

prompt: A class measures the length of every pupil's foot, in centimetres. Which graph should display the results?
options: a histogram, with the bars touching
a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
answer: a histogram, with the bars touching
explain: Work it as steps 3 and 4 did for finger length: foot length is measured, so any value in between is possible and the classes run straight into one another. That is a histogram, with the bars touching. Gaps between bars are for data that comes in separate groups.

optionNotes.option: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
optionNotes.why: Gaps say there is nothing in between, but every foot length between two values is possible, so the bars must touch.
A pie chart shows shares of a whole; it cannot show how a measurement is spread across a range.

twin.prompt: A class records whether each pupil can roll their tongue. Which graph should display the results?
options: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
a histogram, with the bars touching
twin.answer: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars
twin.explain: Work it as steps 1 and 2 did for earlobes: tongue rolling falls into two separate groups, can or cannot, with nothing in between. So the bars stand apart: a bar chart, with gaps between the bars.

md: A percentage of a class is the group as a share of the whole: the group on top, the whole class underneath, then multiply by 100. The class size is often not printed: add every bar to find it. A part of a class always comes out under 100%.

stem: What percentage of the class in the histogram is shorter than 160 cm? Give your answer to 1 decimal place. [2]

steps.decision: Read the bars that end at or before 160 cm against the gridlines, one pupil per line.
The question never gives the total: add every bar.
The group on top, the whole class underneath. Writing this down earns the first mark.
Check: part of the class, so under 100%.

prompt: In a class of 20 pupils, 7 are left-handed. What percentage of the class is left-handed?
explain: Steps 3 and 4 of the worked answer: the group on top, the whole class underneath, then multiply by 100. Here 7 ÷ 20 × 100 = 35%. Check: a part of the class, so under 100%.

twin.prompt: In a class of 24 pupils, 6 are left-handed. What percentage of the class is left-handed?
twin.explain: The group on top, the whole class underneath: 6 ÷ 24 × 100 = 25%. A part of the class, so under 100%.

caption: Most differences between people come from both.

md: Variation has a **genetic** basis and an **environmental** basis. **Genetic:** a **mutation** is a **random change in the number of chromosomes or the structure of a gene**, so it can make something new. In **sexual reproduction**, meiosis gives every gamete a different mix of alleles and fertilisation joins two of them, so each child has a new combination.
**Environmental:** your surroundings shape how you develop. **Diet** affects **height**, for example. Most characteristics depend on both genes and environment.

stem: Explain how sexual reproduction and mutation each give variation a genetic basis. [2]

steps.working: In meiosis each gamete gets a different mix of alleles, and fertilisation joins two gametes, so every child inherits a new combination.
steps.decision: Sexual reproduction first: it reshuffles alleles the parents already have.

steps.working: A random change in the structure of a gene, or in the number of chromosomes, can produce a characteristic that neither parent had.
steps.decision: Then the other cause: something new, by chance, in the genetic material itself.

prompt: A random change in one of a pupil's genes gives her a characteristic that neither parent shows. Which cause of variation is this?
explain: Step 2 of the worked answer: a random change in the structure of a gene, or in the number of chromosomes, is a mutation, and it can produce something no parent had. Sexual reproduction only reshuffles alleles the parents already have, and the environment does not change genes. So it is a mutation.

optionNotes.why: Sexual reproduction reshuffles alleles the parents already carry; a random change in a gene itself is a mutation.
The environment acts on the body during life and does not change genes; a change in a gene is genetic.

twin.prompt: Each child of two parents inherits a new combination of their alleles. Which cause of variation is this?
twin.explain: Step 1 of the worked answer: meiosis mixes the alleles in each gamete and fertilisation joins two gametes, so every child gets a new combination. Nothing in a gene has changed, so it is not a mutation. That is sexual reproduction.

md: Cuttings taken from one plant all have the **same genes**. Grow two of them with different amounts of water and they reach different heights, so the difference can only have come from the **environment**. Identical twins, who come from one fertilised egg, show the same thing in people.

title: What this clip will not cover
md: Clips made for other boards cover the causes of variation, but those exams do not ask about **continuous** and **discontinuous** variation or which graph goes with each. CCEA does, so that part comes from this lesson. Types of mutation, if they appear, are not on this specification.

stem: Identical twins were brought up apart. One grew to 171 cm and the other to 163 cm. Explain why their heights are different. [2]

steps.working: Identical twins come from one fertilised egg that split, so everything they inherited is exactly the same.
steps.decision: Start with what they share: they cannot differ in anything they inherited.

steps.working: So the 8 cm difference must be caused by the environment, such as a better diet for the taller twin.
steps.decision: Only the environment is left to cause it: name a factor to make the point real.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Variation"
why: A short lesson on the causes of variation, made for another exam board, after the worked answer. Watch it, then answer the next check without going back.

prompt: Two cuttings from the same plant grow to different heights. Because they have the same ______, the difference must be caused by the environment.
answer: genes | gene | genetic material | dna | alleles | genetic makeup | genetic make-up | genetic information | genotype | genetic code | same genes | the same genes | same dna | the same dna | same genetic material | the same genetic material | same alleles | the same alleles | same genetic information | the same genetic information | same gene | the same gene
explain: Cuttings from one plant, like the identical twins in step 1, inherited exactly the same: the same genes. A difference between two things with the same genes cannot come from the genes, so only the environment is left, here the water. So the word is genes.

twin.prompt: Identical twins grow up apart and one becomes much heavier than the other. The difference in their mass is caused by the ______.
twin.answer: environment | the environment | environmental factors | diet | their diet
twin.explain: Identical twins inherited exactly the same genes, as step 1 said, so a difference between them cannot be genetic. Only the environment is left, such as diet. So the word is environment.

md:
Tell **continuous** variation (any value in a range) from **discontinuous** (separate groups), with an example of each.
Choose the graph and say why: a **histogram** with bars touching, or a **bar chart** with gaps.
Read a bar chart or histogram and turn a count into a **percentage** of the class.
Name the genetic causes, **mutation** and **sexual reproduction**, and define a mutation.
Explain an **environmental** cause, and why most characteristics depend on both.

Variation turns up as short parts of a bigger B2 question, mostly on the Foundation paper: the type of variation or a graph reading, then the reason or the percentage. **The twist** (Summer 2023 Higher): a question about dog whelks ended by asking what type of variation their shell colour shows. Ask one question: counted into groups, or measured on a scale? A few colours, so discontinuous.
